standard.title: Food properties and presentation
standard.description: analyse how properties of foods determine preparation and presentation techniques when designing solutions for healthy eating
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain how the characteristics of foods influence selection and preparation for healthy eating (AC9TDE6K04). They understand that food characteristics matter for healthy eating but have not yet analysed how specific food properties (sensory properties, nutrient retention) determine preparation and presentation techniques.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how the properties of foods — including sensory properties (flavour, texture, appearance, aroma) and nutrient value — determine the selection of preparation and presentation techniques when designing solutions for healthy eating.

nodes.label: Food properties that matter
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the sensory properties and nutritional properties of foods that influence how they should be prepared
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least two sensory properties (e.g. flavour, texture, appearance, aroma) and explain how each is affected by preparation
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish between sensory properties and nutritional properties; explain how preparation techniques can enhance one while diminishing another (e.g. roasting improves flavour but may reduce nutrient value)
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians prepare foods to improve edibility — for example, leaching toxins from seeds or using specific cooking methods that preserve nutritional value
Compare how the same food's properties are valued differently across cultures — what one culture considers desirable texture or flavour may differ from another
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who know only two sensory properties will not be able to explain preparation trade-offs at Node 2 — selecting between techniques requires understanding how multiple properties respond differently to different methods, and that sensory and nutritional properties can pull in opposite directions.
success_criteria: Names at least two sensory properties of food
Explains how at least one property is affected by preparation

response_modes.reason: Food properties must be accumulated across types before students can reason about how preparation affects them. Students who only know two sensory properties will not be able to explain preparation trade-offs at Node 2. More food examples with different property profiles build the repertoire needed.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations preparation methods and cross-cultural property valuation directions are genuinely rich — they reveal that food properties are not objective facts but are valued differently across cultural contexts, which is a substantive insight beyond the minimum.

nodes.label: How preparation techniques affect properties
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how different preparation techniques impact sensory properties and nutrient retention
nodes.minimum_width: Given a preparation technique, explain how it changes at least one sensory property and its effect on nutrient value
nodes.typical_width: Compare multiple techniques (e.g. stir-frying vs steaming vs boiling) and analyse how each affects flavour, texture, appearance and nutrient retention differently; explain how a recipe can be modified to enhance health benefits
wider: Analyse food preparation techniques from Asian cultures (e.g. stir-frying, steaming, poaching) and their impact on nutrient retention compared to Western techniques
Investigate how traditional wood selection for roasting and smoking complements flavour in First Nations cooking
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat preparation techniques as generic 'cooking methods' rather than deliberate choices that transform specific properties will not be able to select and justify techniques at Node 3 — design for healthy eating requires knowing how each technique affects both sensory appeal and nutrient value.
success_criteria: Explains how a preparation technique changes at least one sensory property
Identifies whether the technique improves or reduces nutrient value

response_modes.reason: Students who think of preparation techniques as simply 'cooking methods' rather than as deliberate choices that transform food properties will not be able to design solutions for healthy eating at Node 3. Seeing how different techniques produce different outcomes across multiple food types and cultural traditions builds the analytical framework needed.

nodes.label: Designing for healthy eating
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select and justify preparation and presentation techniques based on food properties when designing solutions for healthy eating
nodes.minimum_width: Given a healthy eating goal, select a preparation technique and explain why it suits the food's properties and the health objective
nodes.typical_width: Design a food solution that balances sensory appeal with nutritional goals; justify technique and presentation choices by referencing specific food properties; modify an existing recipe to improve its health benefits while maintaining appeal
wider: Compare food design solutions across cultures — how different traditions balance health, flavour and presentation using different techniques and different foods
Design a food solution for a specific dietary requirement and evaluate how preparation techniques support both the nutritional need and sensory experience
success_criteria: Selects a preparation technique appropriate for the food and the health objective
Justifies the choice by referencing specific food properties

response_modes.reason: Designing for healthy eating requires students to draw on food property knowledge (Node 1) and preparation technique analysis (Node 2) simultaneously — selecting a technique requires knowing both what it does to sensory properties and how it affects nutrient retention. Students who have learned these separately often design without considering both dimensions.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The cross-cultural food design comparison and specific dietary requirement directions offer advancing students genuinely complex design problems — balancing nutritional science, sensory appeal and cultural appropriateness requires more sophisticated design reasoning than a single-context brief.
